extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, sociology/criminology students and researchers, and critical journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate the processes, news-values and institutional relations by which newspapers produce crime news (with a focus on 'mugging' as a case). Emphasis on source access, framing, news cycles and the role of primary definers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media as transformation (not mere reproduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: This process is neither totally free and unconstrained, nor is it a simple, direct reproduction. It is a transformation; and such transformations require active 'work' on the part of the media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media translate unfamiliar statements of primary definers into the paper's 'public idiom', making definitions of the powerful part of taken-for-granted public reality. Examine how journalists rephrase, condense, contextualise and domesticate source statements rather than simply reprinting them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public idiom and editorial voice
rubrics_metrics.description: A newspaper has a 'public idiom' — the code or mode of address customarily used by that paper — and an editorial voice which can express opinion or claim to 'take the public voice'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how the paper's idiom shapes translations of source claims, and whether editorials are used to assert 'we believe...' as an act of 'making the public voice'. Distinguish between expressing the paper's own views and claiming to represent public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorialising as legitimating and mobilising
rubrics_metrics.description: The press can editorialise — speak its own mind — to legitimate actions of controllers or to mobilise public opinion on behalf of particular actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for editorials that either endorse state action (legitimation) or call for stronger measures (mobilisation). Note the mediating position between public sentiment and institutions of social control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mediating/connective role of the media
rubrics_metrics.description: Media command the passage between those 'in the know' and the structured ignorance of the general public, serving as a critical mediating and connective role in formation of public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how media act as gatekeepers and interpreters — not weakened but enhanced by structural independence — and how that passage shapes what the public is permitted to know.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency toward ideological closure
rubrics_metrics.description: The routine structures and practices of the media serve to 'frame' events within dominant interpretative paradigms, promoting prevailing definitions of the powerful and the dominant ideology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse structural tendencies (not individual malice) that close debate; assess framing devices that keep public discourse within a limited 'range' of acceptable viewpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counter-tendency depends on organised counter-definers
rubrics_metrics.description: Counter-tendencies to ideological closure depend on organised and articulate sources which generate counter-definitions of the situation (social groups/collectivities as infrastructure of ideologies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether alternatives exist: are there organised, articulate groups (or substantial minorities) with legitimacy or capacity to win legitimacy through struggle? Their existence reduces closure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access and legitimacy of counter-definers
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether alternative definers (e.g., trade unions) can secure a hearing depends on whether they have access, legitimacy and whether they frame their claims within acceptable consensus rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess if counter-definers 'play within the rules' (e.g., reasonable arguments) and thus get balanced reporting, or are labelled 'extremist'/'irrational' and excluded. Example: T.U.C. vs. unofficial strike action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structured silences and omitted questions
rubrics_metrics.description: The media favour certain ways of setting up topics and maintain strategic areas of silence; many structured forms of communication are so embedded they are invisible unless explicitly interrogated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use critical questions: 'What, other than what has been said about this topic, could be said?' 'What questions are omitted?' 'Why do certain recurring question-forms presuppose particular answers?' This reveals hidden frames and power.

rubrics_metrics.name: News as mapping disruptions to social consensus (crime's newsworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: News is shaped by a conception of society as a 'consensus'; events that interrupt consensual calm (e.g., crime) are made news because they evoke threats to — and reaffirm — consensual morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how reports present events as boundary violations that dramatise and reassert societal values; crime is news because it dramatizes the frontier of acceptable behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary definers' dominance in crime reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: In crime news the media are heavily dependent on institutions of crime control (police, Home Office, courts) which form a near-monopoly as sources of crime news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess sourcing patterns: extent of police/Home Office/court statements versus independent or offender voices. High dependence signals reproduction of controller definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust-based relations between journalists and police
rubrics_metrics.description: The journalist derives crime material from formal/informal relations dependent on 'trust' between police and crime correspondents; betrayal of trust can dry up information flows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the reciprocity and informal agreements that grant privileged access; consider how this shapes content and limits adversarial reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional authority of Home Office and judiciary
rubrics_metrics.description: The Home Office is accredited because of responsibility to Parliament; judges' pronouncements carry symbolic authority — they act as 'ventriloquists' for moral order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note how institutional status is used as credentialing evidence in reports and how judicial remarks are highlighted (e.g., sentencing day) as newsworthy anchors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crime is less open to competing definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Crime is less open to alternative definitions because criminals are illegitimate/unorganised; organised reformers often share the same basic definition (returning offender to fold), so debate stays within controllers' terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate presence/absence of alternative framings (e.g., structural causes, restorative perspectives). Absence implies one-dimensional, pragmatic coverage limited to 'what can be done'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical crime-news formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Three typical formats cover most crime stories: (1) police-statement-based reports (investigation and reconstruction), (2) 'state of the war against crime' reports (statistics + official interpretation), (3) court-case stories (trial, sentencing, judge's remarks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When coding or assessing crime coverage, categorize pieces by these formats and note which dominates; each format privileges particular definers and framings.

rubrics_metrics.name: News values that determine selection and prominence
rubrics_metrics.description: The same structure of 'news values' (novelty, topicality, competitiveness, violence, bizarre, elite/famous person, negative consequences) determines which crime stories receive special attention and the relative attention they get.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly code for these news values when judging selection: novelty lifts items into visibility; other values sustain news-life as novelty fades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty as the initial lifting mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty is often sufficient to bring discrete/common events into news (e.g., labelling disparate incidents as 'mugging'); novelty has the most limited life-span among news values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether initial coverage relies on a 'new' label supplied by primary definers and how long novelty sustains prominence before other values must supplement it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Violence as supreme news value
rubrics_metrics.description: Violence represents negative consequences and is often at or near the summit of news attention; murder — especially of a policeman — is particularly newsworthy as the ultimate rupture of social order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure intensity of violent content and note that presence of gratuitous or instrumental violence escalates news prominence. Violence is a powerful sustaining value after novelty fades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bizarre as an augmenting news value
rubrics_metrics.description: Bizarre reports — unusual, eccentric, grotesque or humorously odd events — can increase news visibility; they subdivide into humorous twists and menacing grotesqueries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code for bizarreness and its subtypes; note that the 'bizarre' can create associative effects and signal wider social concerns (e.g., female violence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elite/famous-person value (context-dependent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories gain news visibility if involving elites or famous people, but this value may be weak or insignificant in some crime topics (e.g., mugging sample showed few such cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider celebrity as a possible augmenting factor but test empirically for the topic under study rather than assuming universal importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label adoption and generative/associative effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The simple attribution of a label (e.g., 'mugging') by primary definers is often sufficient to bring many discrete events into the orbit of news; labels have 'generative and associative' effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace how official labels are adopted and propagated by press; examine associative chains (e.g., linking random incidents to a perceived trend) that expand a topic's news-life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine versus extraordinary reporting and constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Much crime news is routine and brief (court summaries, brief notices), constrained by rules such as sub judice; extraordinary instances are treated at greater length and lifted out against routine background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish routine beat reporting from extended feature/serial coverage; evaluate institutional/legal constraints that shape brevity and content (e.g., presumption of innocence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing through juxtaposition and implied social calculus
rubrics_metrics.description: Juxtapositions (e.g., violent assault 'for 30p') create dissonance and imply a rational calculus about motives and the meaning of violence, shaping public signification of crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine headlines and narrative juxtapositions that implicitly moralize or stigmatise offenders by framing violence as irrational or disproportionate to gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cycle of news-life and augmentation strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'cycle' of news-worthiness exists: novelty initially, then augmentation by other news values (bizarre, violence) to sustain coverage until the story's news-life expires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing longitudinal coverage, map phases (emergence, peak, sustainment, decline) and identify which news values play roles at each phase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visibility amplified by organizational/ideological processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Altering visibility of particular crime items operates in conjunction with organisational/ideological processes (competition among items, novelty, topicality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider newsroom competition, space constraints, and ideological predispositions when explaining why certain crime items are escalated or downplayed.
